nameStory: The ocean quahog gets its name from combining 'ocean' (since it lives in deeper waters offshore) with 'quahog,' a word borrowed from the Narragansett Native American term 'poquauhock' meaning 'hard clam.' Unlike regular quahogs that live in shallow tidal areas, these sturdy clams make their home in the deeper ocean waters.
description: The ocean quahog is a large, edible clam that lives on the ocean floor in deeper waters off New England's coast. These round, sturdy shells can grow larger than two inches across and are covered in a distinctive dark, almost black outer coating. Unlike the familiar quahogs you might dig up at the beach, ocean quahogs live permanently underwater in deeper areas where only commercial fishing boats can reach them with special dredging equipment. They're remarkably long-lived creatures, with some individuals surviving for hundreds of years.

idTips.label: Dark outer coating
idTips.description: The shell has a black or very dark brown leathery coating called the periostracum that feels rough and may flake off in places, revealing lighter shell underneath

idTips.label: Round shell shape
idTips.description: More circular and dome-shaped than regular quahogs, with a distinctly rounded profile when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Smooth interior margin
idTips.description: Inside the shell, the pallial line (the curved line where the clam's body attached) is smooth without the notched indentation found in regular quahogs

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: Mature shells exceed two inches in height and feel substantial and heavy in your hand, often larger than typical quahogs

idTips.label: Thick, sturdy shell
idTips.description: The shell walls are notably thick and robust, making a solid 'thunk' sound when tapped, built to withstand deep ocean pressures

habitat: Ocean quahogs live on sandy or muddy bottoms in deeper coastal waters throughout the North Atlantic, typically too deep for recreational clam digging. In New England waters, they're found offshore where commercial fishing boats harvest them using dredges. You're most likely to encounter their shells washed up on beaches after storms, rather than finding live specimens.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after winter storms, often still retaining their dark outer coating. This is a good time to find well-preserved specimens on beaches.
seasonality.summer: Beach-walking yields the best opportunities to find ocean quahog shells, though the dark coating may be bleached or worn away by sun and surf.
seasonality.fall: Continued opportunities to find shells on beaches, particularly after autumn storms stir up offshore sediments and debris.
seasonality.winter: Storm activity may bring shells to shore, though beach access can be challenging. Shells found in winter are often the freshest specimens.

funFact: One ocean quahog clam named 'Ming' lived for 507 years, making it older than Shakespeare, older than the founding of America, and the longest-lived animal with a known age ever discovered — it was unfortunately killed during the process of determining its age!
confusionNotes: Ocean quahogs are easily confused with regular hard-shell quahogs (littlenecks and cherrystones), but remember the ocean quahog's signature black coat and rounder shape. If you found it by digging in the sand at low tide, it's definitely a regular quahog — ocean quahogs live too deep to dig up by hand.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize there are different types of quahogs, and 'mahogany clam' or 'black clam' at the fish market refers to this deeper-water species. The shells you find on the beach are likely from commercial fishing operations rather than naturally deceased clams, since these animals can live for centuries.
compareHints: Since ocean quahogs are the only species in their genus in New England, compare them to regular hard clams (quahogs) in the Venus clam family. Ocean quahogs are rounder, have that distinctive black outer coating, and lack the notched pallial line inside the shell that regular quahogs have. Think of ocean quahogs as the deep-water cousin of the familiar beach-digging quahog.
